Science Fiction. A literary mode that imagines worlds and futures shaped by scientific discovery, technological innovation, or speculative science. Rather than depicting the impossible as supernatural, as fantasy does, science fiction grounds its speculation in plausible scientific extrapolation: faster-than-light travel, artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, time manipulation, alternate histories, contact with alien civilizations.

Science fiction originated with Mary Shelley's Frankenstein in eighteen eighteen. Shelley imagined scientific ambition creating life through galvanism, leading to catastrophe and exploring technology's ethical costs. Jules Verne and H. G. Wells systematized the form in the late nineteenth century. Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea and Journey to the Center of the Earth featured extraordinary voyages enabled by speculative technology. Wells wrote The Time Machine, The War of the Worlds, and The Island of Doctor Moreau, treating science fiction as social allegory. Time travel, alien invasion, and genetic experimentation became vehicles for exploring class, empire, and scientific ethics.

Hard science fiction prioritizes scientific accuracy and speculation grounded in physics, astronomy, biology. Isaac Asimov and Arthur C. Clarke are exemplars. Soft science fiction emphasizes social, psychological, and cultural speculation, less concerned with technical plausibility and often exploring linguistics, sociology, psychology. Cyberpunk, a late twentieth-century movement, fused computers, virtual reality, corporate power, and dystopian futures. William Gibson exemplified the form. Post-human science fiction explores artificial intelligence, genetic modification, and digital consciousness, questioning the boundaries of humanity itself.

The major themes of science fiction include technological consequences—how technology reshapes society, psychology, and human nature through utopian and dystopian trajectories. Alien encounter explores first contact with non-human intelligence and what meeting the alien reveals about ourselves. Time travel and causality raise temporal paradoxes. If you can change the past, is the future fixed or mutable? Dystopia imagines totalitarian futures, environmental collapse, technological surveillance. Science fiction serves as warning. Space exploration represents the frontier—escape from Earth, colonization of other worlds.

The literary heritage of science fiction begins with pulp magazines. Amazing Stories began in nineteen twenty-six. Science fiction became a popular, commercial form, distinct from high-literary modernism. The Golden Age of science fiction, spanning the nineteen thirties through nineteen forties, emphasized adventure, wonder, and optimism about technological progress. Isaac Asimov and Ray Bradbury were key figures. The New Wave of the nineteen sixties brought literary experimentation and formal innovation with psychological depth. Harlan Ellison, Ursula K. Le Guin, and Samuel R. Delany pioneered this movement. Contemporary science fiction shows mainstream literary integration. Margaret Atwood, N. K. Jemisin, and Ted Chiang represent the form today.

Key concepts in science fiction include worldbuilding—science fiction requires consistent, detailed imaginative worlds where the fictional world is a thought-experiment. The novum is the central speculative innovation that drives narrative—what is imagined differently from our reality? Estrangement makes the familiar strange. By imagining futures or alien worlds, science fiction illuminates our own time.

Science fiction occupies a paradoxical position. It is the most commercially successful literary genre globally, yet often dismissed as low literature by literary establishments. Yet science fiction has profoundly shaped how we imagine technology, the future, and human possibility. Frankenstein is now canonical high literature, but science fiction as a whole remains caught between pulp origins and literary legitimacy. Science fiction's influence on philosophy, cognitive science, and futurism is immense. Scenarios imagined in science fiction shape how we think about artificial intelligence, climate, biotechnology, and space exploration. The genre embodies Enlightenment rationality applied to the future. It asks what if with scientific rigor.
